transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-12-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 43 minutes
Attendees: Sara (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Lina (Redwood Partnerships), Alex (Cobalt CTO), Priya (Cobalt Head of Infra), Mark (Cobalt PM)
Links shared: partner deck (link: https://redwood.ai/partners/deck), SOC2 summary (link: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2), benchmark template (link: https://drive.google.com/redwood-bench)

Summary:
Quick partner intro + discovery to understand CobaltCompute's go-to-market and technical requirements for GPU fleet integrations; primary focus on Dedicated/private deployment options and potential co-sell pilot.

Topics:
- Cobalt's current offering and customer base
- Integration patterns (API, marketplace, dedicated GPU pools)
- Security/compliance needs (SOC2, SSO, KMS)
- Performance benchmarks and pilot scope
- Commercial model and next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Sara: hi everyone thanks for joining, um this is Sara from Redwood, I'm the AE on this region. we also have Diego our solutions engineer and Lina from partnerships. how are you all?
[00:06] Alex: hey Sara, good thanks. Alex here. excited to learn more, appreciate you taking the time.
[00:12] Priya: hi, Priya here, quick note we've got about 40 minutes.
[00:17] Sara: perfect, we'll keep it tight. quick agenda, we'll do intros, you tell us about Cobalt, then Diego will run a quick tech clarifying questions, and we'll finish with next steps. sound good?
[00:27] Mark: yep sounds good.
[00:30] Sara: okay Alex, wanna kick off with a high level on Cobalt's product and go-to-market?
[00:35] Alex: sure. so CobaltCompute provides dedicated GPU clusters as a managed service for small enterprises focused on ML inferencing and video analytics. our customers are mid-market SaaS and some telco partners. we run a multi-tenant orchestration layer and offer both API endpoints and private network peering. we're looking to expand into inference marketplace partnerships and offer a fast path for customers to run large LLMs, like 30B/70B models, and we want to do that with better cost predictability.
[01:05] Diego: when you say multi-tenant, are you running tenant isolation at the hypervisor level or using k8s namespace isolation?
[01:10] Priya: it's a mix, we use k8s + hardware isolation for high tier customers, and we use NVidia MIG on certain shapes. some customers require VPC peering and dedicated subnets.
[01:20] Sara: great perfect, and what are the top three pain points you're hearing from customers about current LLM serving?
[01:27] Alex: latency at scale, cost unpredictability, and model compatibility — vendors or frameworks change and there's constant effort to keep kernels optimized. also compliance asks for audit trails and customer-managed keys.
[01:37] Lina: makes sense. Diego, quick sanity check: would Redwood's Dedicated offering map to their high-tier use case?
[01:42] Diego: yeah, Redwood Dedicated is basically reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput, autoscale options, and can be configured for VPC/private deployments. caveat: workload profile matters a lot — sequence lengths, concurrency, kv-cache behavior, all change the economics.
[01:56] Mark: can you talk about kv cache? we've heard 'KV cache' thrown around but not totally sure how it helps.
[02:02] Diego: sure. KV cache lets you cache prefix tokens and reduce repeated compute for chat-style sessions. some transcription, or sorry some transcriptions call it 'KV cash' haha but it's basically a prefix cache. for long conversations it saves a ton.
[02:14] Alex: interesting, our main ask is to support both hosted marketplace integration and an option to offer Redwood as a managed runtime on our metal. how does the private deploy model work?
[02:23] Sara: Redwood Private has a customer-managed control plane option and an on-prem package. you can run the inference runtime within your VPC or on-prem cluster, and the control plane can either be routed through our hosted control plane or be fully customer-managed depending on compliance.
[02:36] Priya: what about key management? customers often insist on KMS/HSM and we have to show audit logs.
[02:42] Diego: we support KMS integrations and can plug into your cloud KMS or an HSM. audit logs are collected at route/token level and can be forwarded to your SIEM. SOC2 and ISO attestations are available — we'll send the SOC2 summary after.
[02:55] Alex: do you do per-request encryption or is it at rest only?
[03:00] Diego: both. you can use customer-managed keys for at-rest encryption and TLS for in-flight; for additional controls we can isolate network paths via VPC peering.
[03:08] Mark: latency targets — what latency numbers do you regularly hit for 8k context?
[03:13] Diego: it really depends on model architecture and hardware. for a 13B model on A100-like infrastructure you might see median token latency in the low tens of ms, but for 70B models latencies grow. Redwood's runtime selects kernels and quantization paths to optimize, but if you need strict tail-latency SLOs we recommend dedicated capacity.
[03:29] Alex: so would our customers who run 70B choose Redwood hosted or bring-your-own infra?
[03:35] Sara: typically, early-stage customers use hosted for speed-to-value. larger customers with strict SLAs or data residency often prefer Dedicated or Private. Redwood's routing can also fallback to smaller model variants to meet SLOs if capacity constrained.
[03:48] Priya: we care a lot about pricing predictability. how are unit economics surfaced?
[03:52] Lina: our console breaks down token-level cost, latency and per-route metrics so you can tie features to cost. Diego, maybe talk about Optimize?
[03:59] Diego: Redwood Optimize suggests batching and quantization profiles for your workload, and we surface the estimated cost savings. for customers with bursty workloads, autoscale plus burst pools help reduce commit costs.
[04:11] Alex: what's the integration surface — do you expose a REST API and an SDK?
[04:15] Sara: yes, REST + SDKs for python/node, streaming responses, function/tool calling, and embeddings endpoints. integration is straightforward — we also provide a model catalog with performance profiles.
[04:24] Mark: how are model updates handled? we have customers who need model pinning and gradual rollouts.
[04:29] Diego: we support version pinning and can do canary rollouts and automatic rollback policies if quality degrades. we also tie into evals and prompt sets to detect regressions.
[04:39] Alex: switching gears — for a partner pilot, what would success criteria look like?
[04:44] Sara: usually: 1) confirm performance SLOs for a defined model set at target QPS, 2) validate security/compliance integration (KMS, audit logs), 3) prove unit economics vs their current setup, and 4) define a co-sell/marketplace go-to-market plan.
[04:58] Priya: timeline? our Q1 bookings look promising and we'd like to have a pilot infra-ready by late Jan. is that feasible?
[05:05] Diego: feasible, yes. rough phases: design/requirements (2 weeks), integration + benchmarking (3-4 weeks), pilot validation (2 weeks). so late Jan is realistic if we start early Dec.
[05:18] Alex: one blocker — some customers require SOC2 Type II and local data residency in EU. can you host EU-region private deployments?
[05:26] Sara: yes, Redwood has EU regions and Private deployments can be set up in-region. SOC2 Type II docs will be in the packet we send.
[05:33] Mark: curious about hardware — do you recommend particular GPU vendors? customers ask about Ampere vs Hopper.
[05:39] Diego: the runtime supports both; choice depends on your model and perf/cost tradeoffs. Hopper has advantages for really large models and sequence lengths, Ampere is cost-effective for mid-sized models. we'll help benchmark.
[05:50] Alex: competitors — we've had calls with Lambda and Paperspace; how does Redwood differentiate?
[05:55] Sara: we focus on inference economics + unified operational tooling across hosted/dedicated/private. we also offer deeper workload-aware batching and KV caching plus first-class observability and rollouts.
[06:05] Priya: any known limitations we should flag?
[06:08] Diego: one is that very custom kernels or unsupported model ops require some engineering to onboard; quantization may be model-sensitive so we'll validate. also, if your workload is extremely latency-sensitive at tails, you'll need to plan capacity carefully.
[06:21] Alex: on onboarding cost model — do you do revenue share, commit contracts, or marketplace revenue?
[06:26] Lina: we have multiple commercial options: usage-based for hosted, reserved/commit contracts for Dedicated, enterprise licensing for Private, and marketplace revenue share for integrations. we can propose a pilot financial model.
[06:37] Mark: for the pilot, we'd likely want a co-branded marketplace listing and a technical integration that allows our customers to pick Redwood-backed runtimes. is that supported?
[06:46] Sara: yes, we have partner marketplace integrations; we can discuss listing requirements and support for co-branding.
[06:51] Alex: security follow-ups — can you outline the audit log retention and SIEM integration?
[06:56] Diego: logs are at token/route level, retention configurable, and we support forwarding to common SIEMs via syslog or cloud logging sinks. we'll include details in the security packet.
[07:07] Mark: do you support SAML/SSO for enterprise customers?
[07:10] Sara: yes SSO (SAML/OIDC), RBAC and org-level controls are supported.
[07:15] Priya: from a networking perspective, we need clear docs on VPC peering, egress rules, and egress IPs for allowlisting.
[07:22] Diego: we'll provide a network integration guide with example firewall rules and egress IP ranges.
[07:27] Alex: let's talk about benchmarks — what do you need from us to run a representative benchmark?
[07:31] Diego: sample models (or model names), typical sequence lengths, expected concurrency and QPS, sample prompt distribution, and any cost constraints. we'll share a benchmark template.
[07:41] Alex: ok we'll provide that. also, are there limits on model licenses — like commercial vs non-commercial?
[07:47] Sara: licensing depends on the model and provider; we help customers navigate open models and vendor-licensed models but licensing clarity is essential before production.
[07:55] Mark: customers increasingly ask for CPU fallbacks if GPU exhausted — is that a pattern you support?
[07:59] Diego: you can configure routing policies that fallback to cheaper model variants or CPU-based runtimes, though performance will differ.
[08:07] Priya: any reference customers in the telco space?
[08:10] Lina: we have a couple of telco references — we'll include anonymized case studies in the follow-up.
[08:16] Alex: perfect. quick commercial question — if we run Redwood runtime on our hardware, how does billing work?
[08:22] Sara: typically a platform fee plus support for Private deployments; if we run under a marketplace, revenue share terms apply. for Dedicated we do reserved commits. we can propose options after the initial scoping.
[08:34] Mark: from our side, success means: clear architecture docs, sample benchmark showing cost parity or improvement, security sign-off, and a joint go-to-market plan.
[08:45] Sara: that's helpful. Diego, anything we should demo in a follow-up SE deep-dive?
[08:50] Diego: i'd demo the runtime config for autoscale, show KV cache behavior on a chat workload, and run a quick quantization comparison. also walk through the network/SSO integration.
[08:59] Alex: sounds good. one last question — do you have limits on supported frameworks? we use a mix of PyTorch and some ONNX pipelines.
[09:05] Diego: we support PyTorch and ONNX-backed models; some custom ops in ONNX may need work but it's usually doable.
[09:12] Priya: ok great.
[09:14] Speaker 2: (inaudible)
[09:17] Sara: okay we'll wrap with next steps: i'll send the partner packet (deck + SOC2), Diego will share the benchmark template, and we'll schedule the SE architecture deep-dive for the week of 2026-12-14. Alex you'll share the QPS and model list by 2026-12-08. any other asks?
[09:31] Alex: no that's it, thanks all.
[09:34] Sara: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email.

End of transcript

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings (e.g., 'KV cash' for KV cache), some speaker margins are approximate, minor punctuation missing as typical of automated transcripts.
